**What you already know:** In P.1 and P.2 you learnt about accidents, safety and transport. In P.6 you learn the **English used to talk about road safety** — the vocabulary, the must/should structures, adjectives and adverbs, and the conjunctions *when, because* and *so … that*.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: use road-safety vocabulary correctly
describe how to use the road safely
pronounce and write words with the **'l'** and **'r'** sounds correctly
use *must, mustn't … unless, should not, as soon as, may, should always*
use *because, when, so … that* to give reasons
read and write texts, poems and dialogues about road safety

blocks.x: Rules for using the road safely

Walk on the **right-hand side** facing oncoming traffic where there is no pavement · use a **side path or pavement** where there is one · **look right, look left and look right again** before crossing · cross at the **zebra crossing** or where you can see clearly · never cross in front of or behind a parked vehicle · never play or run in the road · wear **bright clothing** at night · obey the **traffic police** and the traffic lights · wear a **seat belt** in a vehicle and a **helmet** on a motorcycle · never board or leave a moving vehicle · do not put your hand or head out of a moving vehicle.

head: Structure

rows: *The boy crossed the road **as soon as** it was clear.*

blocks.x: Causes of road accidents

Careless and **over-speeding** drivers · **drunken driving** · using a phone while driving · **poor vehicles** — bad brakes and worn tyres · **bad roads** with potholes, no humps or no markings · careless pedestrians crossing without looking · children playing in the road · overloading vehicles · driving at night without lights · animals straying onto the road · riding without a helmet · ignoring road signs and traffic lights.

**What you already know:** You have argued for and against ideas in class. In P.6 you learn the **language of a formal debate** — the roles, the motion, the points of order, and the structures *even though, although* and *if*.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: name the people in a debate and the work of each
read, interpret and formulate a motion
speak for or against a motion using proper language
raise a point of order, information or inquiry correctly
write points and take notes during a debate
use direct and indirect speech and the structures *even though, although, if*

blocks.x: **Debate:** A formal discussion in which two sides argue for and against a motion before an audience.
**Motion:** The statement that is being debated. It always begins with **"That …"** — for example, *"That girls should be given more chances in education than boys."*

sections.title: 2. THE PEOPLE IN A DEBATE AND THEIR WORK

Keeps time and rings a bell to warn or stop a speaker
The first and strongest speaker on each side
Listens, raises points and may vote
Award marks where the debate is a competition

sections.title: 3. THE THREE POINTS AND HOW TO RAISE THEM

head: Point
When it is used
How to say it
rows: When a rule is broken — a speaker abuses another, goes off the motion, or exceeds the time
*"Mr Chairperson, I rise on a **point of order**. The speaker is insulting…"*
When you can give a correct fact the speaker has got wrong
*"Mr Chairperson, on a **point of information**, the school has 400 pupils, not 200."*
When something needs to be made clear
*"Mr Chairperson, on a **point of inquiry**, does the motion mean all pupils or only P.7?"*

blocks.x: **The rule:** stand up, address the **chairperson**, state which point you are raising, be brief, and sit down when the chairperson tells you to.
Opening
*"Mr/Madam Chairperson, honourable members of the house, ladies and gentlemen, I greet you all. I stand here to **support (or oppose)** the motion which says that…"*
Giving points
*"My first point is that…" · "Furthermore…" · "In addition…" · "Moreover…" · "For example…" · "This is because…"*
Disagreeing politely
*"The previous speaker said…, but I disagree because…" · "Even though my opponent says…, the truth is…" · "I would like to correct the previous speaker…"*
Closing
*"With those few words, Mr Chairperson, I beg to move (or oppose) the motion. Thank you."*
Rules of good debating

Address the **chairperson**, not your opponent directly · attack the **point, never the person** · keep to the **motion** · keep within the **time** · speak loudly and clearly · stand up straight and look at the audience · listen when others are speaking · accept the chairperson's ruling.

head: Structure
Example
rows: ***Even though** the previous speaker said father buys clothes, mother loves me more.*
*She argued out her points **although** people did not accept them.*
***If** I **were** the chairperson, I **would** chase Zika from the debate for misbehaviour.*

blocks.x: **Note:** *even though* and *although* both show contrast and are followed by a **complete idea**. In **If 2** we use *were* for every person — *If I **were** you…*

blocks.x: **The rules:** the tense moves **one step back**; pronouns change; *today → that day*, *here → there*, *this → that*; questions become *whether/if* statements; commands become *to + verb*.

**Before the debate:** read the motion carefully and be sure which side you are on · **research** — ask teachers, read books, listen to radio · write your points in **short phrases**, not full paragraphs · put the **strongest point first** · think of what the other side will say and prepare an answer.
**During the debate:** write down each speaker's **main point** in a few words · mark the points you can answer · note any wrong facts so you can raise a **point of information**.
**A sample motion and points**

**Motion: "That television is more useful to a pupil than radio."**  **For:** you see as well as hear · programmes show experiments and places · it teaches good English through pictures and speech. **Against:** it is expensive and needs electricity · it wastes study time · radio is portable and can be used anywhere.

**What you already know:** You can name the members of your family. In P.6 you learn the **full family vocabulary in English**, how to draw and read a **family tree**, and the grammar of **prepositions, adverbs (*just* and *already*) and adjectives**.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: describe family relationships using the correct words
explain the relationship between any two members of a family
draw and interpret a family tree
use prepositions, the adverbs *just* and *already*, and adjectives correctly
read and interpret information about population
write compositions and poems about the family

A dictionary is a book that lists words in alphabetical order and gives information about them. Any four of: spelling, meaning, pronunciation, stress, part of speech, plural form, origin, example sentence.

A **thesaurus** is a book that gives words of **similar meaning (synonyms)** and opposites. A dictionary explains **what a word means**, while a thesaurus offers **other words you could use instead**.
apple, banana, mango, orange, pear
stamp, stand, star, state, stay
chair, chalk, cheese, chief, child
Guide words are the two words at the top of a dictionary page: the **first** word on that page and the **last** word on that page.
**feast** is on that page. *Fast* comes before *father*, and *feed* and *fault* fall outside the range.
**n.** — noun; **v.** — verb; **adj.** — adjective; **adv.** — adverb; **pl.** — plural.
It tells you the **spelling** (quick), the **pronunciation** /kwɪk/, that it is an **adjective**, and its **meaning** — fast, taking a short time.
An **acronym**. Examples: **UNEB**, **NEMA** (also UWA, NGO, AIDS).
**doesn't it?** · **is she?** · **aren't I?**
cheap → **expensive**; arrive → **depart**; polite → **rude**; shallow → **deep**; ancient → **modern**.
happy → **unhappy**; possible → **impossible**; legal → **illegal**; agree → **disagree**; behave → **misbehave**.
tall — taller — **tallest**; big — bigger — **biggest**; happy — happier — **happiest**; expensive — more expensive — **most expensive**; good — better — **best**; bad — worse — **worst**.
Peach comes **before** people, and people comes **after** peach.

Any five of: it gives correct spellings; it explains new words; it shows pronunciation; it gives the part of speech; it improves vocabulary and composition; it settles arguments about meaning; it helps in reading and research.
**Marble**, because after *mar-* we compare the fourth letter: **b** comes before **k**.
*Learner's sentence,* for example: *A dictionary is the **most useful** book in the classroom.*
Any three words falling between *sound* and *spelling* alphabetically, for example **sounds, speech, spell** (also *speaker, special*).

*Learner's paragraph.* It should tell the pupil to know the first letter of the word, open the dictionary near that letter, use the **guide words** at the top of the page, follow the letters one by one, and then read the meaning and the part of speech.
